entries.title: MLB restricts dugout iPads to bar use of AI to make game decisions
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Major League Baseball is restricting iPad usage in dugouts to prevent the tablets from running artificial intelligence to help make strategy decisions, and former reliever Adam Ottavino said the New York Mets' use of technology helped prompt the move.</p><p>The tablets have access to video and league-provided data, and also included a custom tab where teams could access other programs. MLB made the custom tabs inaccessible to teams starting Wednesday night, when the second half of the season started.</p><p>"In many cases, the custom tab had expanded the use of the dugout iPads beyond their originally intended purpose to include recommendations regarding substitutions, pitch calling, and other in-game decisions traditionally made by players and coaches," MLB executive vice president of baseball operations Morgan Sword wrote in a June 11 memo to general managers, assistant GMs and video coordinators.</p><p>The memo, first reported by The Athletic, was obtained by The Associated Press.</p><p>"I read the article and I was like, I can't believe what I'm seeing. Teams are making decisions off of AI? Man, that's just crazy," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said.</p><p>Ottavino said on his YouTube livestream "Baseball & Coffee" that the Mets had been using AI and cited spending by team owner Steve Cohen on the software. Ottavino pitched for the Mets from 2022-24 and is now a broadcaster on the New York Yankees' YES Network.</p><p>"The Mets were actually the team, the main team, that got cracked down on," Ottavino said. "They had an AI program that was very expensive apparently and they were bragging about it a little bit early on in this — the year. Some of the coaches that I know were talking about it from around the league and they had basically an AI program helping them pick pitches and I think some other stuff."</p><p>"But MLB got wind of it and nipped that right in the bud, so apparently they weren't the only team, but I knew about it from the Mets angle," he said. "They tried to throw some money at the situation. Steve ponied up for — I think this program from what I heard was several hundred thousand dollars to have."</p><p>The Mets did not comment when asked whether they had a response.</p><p>A review by the competition committee found clubs had been compliant with the regulations.</p><p>"Instituting this prohibition beginning with the second half of the season is intended to provide clubs that have relied on the custom tab with appropriate lead-time to make any necessary adjustments," Sword wrote.</p><p>Toronto Blue Jays manager John Schneider called it "a little weird to kind of see the whole report on it, where you can do things kind of in real time that can sway your decision one way or another."</p><p>"I think the biggest thing is calling pitches and kind of seeing how that can evolve in real time via technology," he said.</p><p>MLB started a pilot program allowing use of iPads in dugouts with restrictions late in the 2015 season and expanded their use in 2016 under a deal with Apple. Video was eliminated in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season following the Houston Astros' sign-stealing scandal, then returned in 2021.</p><p>"It hasn't impacted us at all but I know AI is entering our arena for sure," Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. "It's entering everyone's arena. You better get on it, or you're going to get rolled over by it."<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox' rout of Toronto 'stokes the flames' for red-hot offense after All-Star break
entries.summary: <p>TORONTO — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> hitters picked up where they left off before the All-Star break, pounding the Blue Jays 12-4 on Friday to pull a half game ahead in the American League Central and match a season-high at six games over .500 (51-45).</p><p>Catcher Kyle Teel tagged an RBI double during a five-run second inning that saw Braden Montgomery and Chase Meidroth knock in two more, before Sam Antonacci’s two-run rainbow of a home run over the right-field wall.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">SAM ANTONACCI 💥 <a href="https://t.co/50uvhFI6Yz">pic.twitter.com/50uvhFI6Yz</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2078266662839574634?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Colson Montgomery cleared a loaded set of bases with a double in the fifth, and Braden Montgomery did the same with his first career triple in the seventh. </p><p>Every Sox starter had a hit as they piled 12 on the last-place Jays.</p><p>"That just kind of stokes the flames," the latter Montgomery said. "We've always got this fire in us, but add a little bit of oxygen to the fire every now and again, where we get more excited to keep going, keep the foot on the pedal."</p><p>Manager Will Venable said "slugging and scoring runs is a big part of our identity, so to come out and do that means a lot."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">tacked on 4️⃣ more ✅ <a href="https://t.co/0RAmATwVzI">pic.twitter.com/0RAmATwVzI</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2078296186012725678?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Sox starter Anthony Kay labored through four innings, giving up two runs on two hits and three walks, with five strikeouts. He also hit his MLB-leading 17th and 18th batters of the year.</p><p>All-Star <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mlb/2026/07/14/white-sox-miguel-vargas-strikes-blow-for-chicago-with-all-star-hr" >Miguel Vargas</a> exited the game after getting plunked on the hand in the eighth, "but he was fine," Venable said. </p><h3>No derby concerns</h3><p>After Munetaka Murakami’s nine-homer outing failed to get him out of the first round of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/13/mlb-all-star-munetaka-murakami-white-sox-home-run-derby-kyle-schwarber-phillies-dylan-cease-jays" >Home Run Derby</a>, the slugging rookie arrived in Toronto looking for his first dinger in game action since May 27, before the hamstring injury that cost him six weeks. He went 1-for-4 with a walk and strikeout in Friday's beatdown.</p><p>Venable said he’s not worried about Murakami’s Derby action affecting the slugger’s form in the second half, brushing aside the common notion in many baseball circles that the free-swinging spectacle can throw off hitters' mechanics.</p><p>“I’m hoping that it helps Mune’s swing, after some time off, to be able to get some ><u>a painfully spectacular catch</u></a> last month at Yankee Stadium. entries.title: Skylar Diggins remains out but says conversations about role moving forward
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> offense was clicking again Friday.</p><p>Five players scored in double figures as they got a much-needed 96-82 victory against the Sparks at Wintrust Arena. But point guard <b>Skylar Diggins</b> only could watch as she continued to manage the discomfort in her right knee.</p><p>Diggins clarified that the issue stems from knee surgery she had last October. She has been doing physical therapy and working with the Sky’s medical staff but hasn’t practiced and doesn’t have a timeline for her return.</p><p>‘‘All I can say is I’ve been progressing day by day,’’ Diggins said before the game. ‘‘Hopefully no setbacks and just playing from there.’’</p><p>In the meantime, Diggins said she has had productive conversations with coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> about her role. Marsh moved Diggins to the bench this month, a decision Diggins said caught her off-guard and wasn’t communicated clearly.</p><p>She since has told Marsh she is prepared to do whatever it takes to ‘‘contribute to winning basketball.’’</p><p>Diggins, who had been playing through discomfort all season, also previously said the Sky lacked some of the resources needed to compete at an elite level. To that end, she called it ‘‘a little disappointing’’ to learn the team <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/17/sky-push-practice-facility-opening-to-november-will-not-move-in-this-season" target="_blank" >won’t move</a> into its new practice facility in Bedford Park this season.</p><p>‘‘I understand setbacks, and things like that happen,’’ Diggins said. ‘‘With a lot of us going through [injuries], it’s just unfortunate because we need a lot of those resources that it was going to provide.</p><p>‘‘We’ve been really grateful for DePaul and Wintrust that let us be here. So we’re going to do the best that we can with the resources that we have.’’</p><h3>Block party</h3><p>Veteran center <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> is moving up in the record book.</p><p>She cracked the top 10 on the WNBA’s career blocks list with 508. She said the keys to a good block are timing and scouting, but the best part is establishing enough of a presence to make opponents think twice before entering the lane.</p><p>Williams sensed the milestone was approaching because she has been keeping an eye on Aces star <b>A’ja Wilson</b>, who ranks eighth.</p><p>She said it ‘‘would be cool’’ to reach the top five. Former Sky great <b>Candace Parker</b> is fifth with 619, so a couple of more healthy seasons might put Williams within reach.</p><h3>Buckets no one saw coming</h3><p>Rookie guard <b>Sydney Taylor</b> also is chasing history — and proving to be the Sky’s best find in recent years.</p><p>Taylor is averaging 13 points, which would be the highest scoring average by an undrafted rookie in WNBA history if she maintains it through the end of the season. She lit it up against the Sparks, scoring 19 points and making four of her seven three-pointers.</p><h3>Cardoso cleared</h3><p>Center <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b> returned to the lineup after missing the Sky’s victory Wednesday against the Storm with knee soreness.</p><p>She looked solid with 13 points, 11 rebounds and three assists in 23 minutes.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: With sights set on World Series, second half means go time for Cubs: ‘There’s some sense of urgency’
entries.summary: <p>It’s go time for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/16/cubs-second-half-preview-brewers-nl-central-standings-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-alex-bregman" >surviving</a> an avalanche of pitching injuries and a monthlong stretch of silent bats during the first half, the two-and-a-half-month sprint to October is here.</p><p>“Now starts kind of a new journey,” shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> said Friday. “There’s some sense of urgency of going out there and playing your best ball right off the bat.</p><p>“There’s no room to get things figured out. We’ve got to be ready today.”</p><p>This team hasn’t been shy about its championship-level expectations: World Series or bust.</p><p>But the Cubs haven’t exactly dominated to this point. Yes, they started the second half in playoff position but five games back of the Brewers in the NL Central.</p><p>What will it take to catch their division rivals? The Cubs say it’s focusing on making the second half a lot less bumpy than the first.</p><p>“That’s all that really matters at the end of the day: if we perform well,” Swanson said. “We can sit here and go through all the scenarios in the world, but what matters is this group stepping up and playing ball that it’s capable of doing.”</p><p>From here on, it’s all about October, all about finding a way to make October last longer than it did last year.</p><p>“We’re starting to average out and become the team we’re supposed to be,” righty reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> said. “But I think there’s a ton of room to grow. … The most important thing is being very hot in September. We’re really starting to show glimpses of it, and it’s starting to show, what kind of team we can be.</p><p>“The most fun baseball you can play is in October. It makes the regular season, honestly, feel kind of meaningless once you do it. But it’s the best.”</p><h3><b>Injury updates</b></h3><h3></h3><p>• Righty pitcher <b>Jameson Taillon</b> will make his long-awaited return from the injured list next week, starting a to-be-determined game during the series with the Tigers. The veteran hasn’t pitched since leaving a June 7 start with a hamstring strain.</p><p>• Righty pitcher <b>Edward Cabrera</b> is throwing off a mound as he comes back from his own strained hamstring, set to throw live batting practice at the start of the Cubs’ road trip next week. Manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Cabrera could “be a viable option” around the second week of August.</p><p>• The Cubs have had to “repeat some steps” in closer <b>Daniel Palencia</b>’s rehab, Counsell said. He’s in Arizona working back from elbow inflammation. That has pushed his estimated return back into the middle of next month.</p><p>• Having tested things out multiple times, utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> is still feeling the hand sprain that sidelined him at the end of June. “That’s definitely going to be longer,” Counsell said of Shaw’s continued absence.</p><p>• Lefty reliever <b>Hoby Milner</b> could return from the IL around Aug. 1 following an appendectomy last month.</p><h3><b>About face</b></h3><p>Swanson was involved in one of the few plays of note in Friday’s 5-2 loss to the Twins, taking a baseball to the face after a throw to second appeared to redirect after hitting the hand of a sliding base-runner.</p><p>Swanson fell to the ground and received a lengthy visit from the trainer, eventually staying in the game.</p><p>He’ll be fine, Counsell reported postgame, but received some wound care.</p><p>“He’s not a dramatic person at all,” second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said, “so I know when he’s going down, there’s something going on. Obviously, a baseball to the face never feels good.</p><p>“He’s a tough guy, but that still doesn’t feel good.”</p><h3><b>Funniest Cub?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Upon hearing a suggestion that third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> is secretly the funniest player in the Cubs’ clubhouse, <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> had to make a correction.</p><p>“I don’t know who told you that,” the All-Star center fielder said. “Not true.”</p><p>OK, so who’s the laugh riot?</p><p>“Breggy’s probably not even top three, man,” he said. “[Taillon, lefty pitcher <b>Shota Imanaga</b>, outfielder <b>Seiya Suzuki</b>]. Seiya is probably the sneakiest funny guy we have.</p><p>“I love Breggy. And he is funny. He’s got good timing. But I don’t think he’s quite earned it yet. He’s earned about everything else in this clubhouse that we could want from him and he could want from us. Funniest? I don’t think he’s there yet.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, items=[{type=Image, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, description=[{items=[It’s not surprising that Hoyer’s front office will have arms at the top of its trade-deadline shopping list, given the Cubs’ first-half injury woes. entries.title: Unsolved murders of police officers require extra attention
entries.summary: <p>I have spent my entire adult life in law enforcement leading officers, supporting their families and surviving the moment every cop fears. In 1987, a bullet struck my ballistic vest and stopped inches from killing me. That impact never leaves you. It is a permanent reminder that every officer who puts on a uniform risks their life for the country they serve.</p><p>That is why I wrote to the president on March 2, and why I am writing again now. My request was simple and rooted in a truth every American should accept: There is no statute of limitations on killing a police officer. Justice should not fade with time, political changes or shifting priorities. Yet across this nation, some officers have been murdered in the line of duty, and their killers have never been brought to justice.</p><p>Two cases show the urgency.</p><p>Officer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/10/28/18474622/fbi-seeking-new-information-about-cold-case-murder-of-maywood-cop" >Thomas T. Wood</a> of the Maywood Police Department was murdered in 2006 while sitting in his patrol SUV. Twenty years later, no arrest has been made.</p><p>Deputy <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/interactive/unresolved/cases/oneal-moore" target="_blank" >Oneal Moore </a>of the Washington Parish Sheriff’s Office in Louisiana was ambushed and killed in 1965. Multiple investigations have been conducted, yet no charges have ever been filed.</p><p>Different eras. Different regions. The same unacceptable outcome.</p><p>When a federal agent is murdered, the U.S. responds with full force and never backs down. That level of commitment should apply to every fallen officer, regardless of jurisdiction. </p><p>I am calling for a permanent, well-funded national cold case unit within the FBI dedicated to unresolved police line-of-duty murders. Not symbolic reviews. Not temporary initiatives. A continuous federal effort to reopen every case, retest all evidence, reexamine every lead and pursue every suspect without exception.</p><p>This is not a partisan issue; it is a moral one.</p><p>President Trump responded to my letter. But the national media has been silent. No coverage. No discussion. No acknowledgment of the issue or the fallen officers behind it. That silence is dangerous. It suggests that justice for murdered police officers is optional — or worse, expendable.</p><p>Unsolved killings of police officers weaken accountability. Families deserve answers. Officers still serving deserve to know their country will not abandon them. The public deserves a justice system that does not look away when those sworn to protect them are murdered.</p><p>I am not requesting special treatment. I am requesting national responsibility.</p><p>I will keep speaking out until someone listens.</p><p><i>Tom Weitzel, retired chief, Riverside Police Department</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7f0000" name="module-7f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Prisoners need better treatment — not new prisons</h3><p>When the Illinois Department of Corrections recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinois.gov/news/release.html?releaseid=32591" target="_blank" >announced</a> a new Logan Correctional Center will be built in Crest Hill, next to the Stateville Correctional Center, I felt deep worry for the women who are behind bars there. As a former Logan inmate, I know firsthand the incarcerated there are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/09/17/female-inmates-sexual-assault-lawsuit-illinois-state-womens-prison" >suffering through conditions</a> the <a class="Link" href="https://idoc.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/idoc/reportsandstatistics/documents/IDOC-Master-Plan-Report-FINAL-MAY-2023-07-12-23-67.pdf" target="_blank" >IDOC itself</a> deems “unsuitable for any population.” </p><p>As I experienced when <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2024/11/19/what-happens-when-prison-closes-dwight-s-demise-10-years-ago-highlights-current-issues" target="_blank" >Dwight Correctional Center closed</a> in 2013, the process of closing a prison is challenging. It affects everyone involved — incarcerated people, guards and loved ones. Nerves are frayed. Tempers can flare. This is why we need a transfer plan now.</p><p>This anticipation, fear and threat of violence mirrors the dynamics of domestic violence relationships — dynamics all too familiar for the people incarcerated at Logan, many of whom are survivors of gender-based violence. Many of those who were transferred out of Dwight still have post-traumatic stress disorder from the experience. </p><p>I am part of <a class="Link" href="https://www.coalitiontodecarcerateil.com/nnp" target="_blank" >No New Prisons Illinois</a>, a campaign endorsed by nearly 50 organizations opposing the state’s billion-dollar plan to rebuild two prisons and urging IDOC and Gov. JB Pritzker’s office to adopt the <a class="Link" href="https://bit.ly/LoganRR" target="_blank" >Logan Transfer Rapid Response Plan</a>. The plan provides a comprehensive list of measures to mitigate the harm of future transfers.</p><p>The plan reflects the experience of currently and formerly incarcerated people who have endured prison closures and know the pitfalls that come when a solid, well-thought-out plan is not in place. </p><p>If the state is committed to the safety and well-being of people incarcerated at Logan, then at least let transfers be conducted humanely and safely. Have a definite plan in place and tell people what to expect before the move.</p><p>The new women's prison is not expected to open until 2030. By this time, 66% of people currently incarcerated at Logan will have served their sentences and will have been released. </p><p>It is my sincerest prayer that people at Logan will not have to suffer the trauma of a transfer. Instead, I pray and ask that the money slated for the building of new prisons is redirected toward reducing the current prison population and improving conditions in the facilities that already exist. </p><p><i>Janet Jackson, fellow, Women’s Justice Institute, and community ambassador, Illinois Prison Project</i></p><h3>Boutros’ criticism is out of order </h3><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros recently <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/wgn-investigates/boutros-blasts-cook-county-judges/" target="_blank" >criticized Cook County judges</a>, claiming they were using trickery in their treatment of violent offenders. In a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/02/doj-boutros-operation-new-dawn-violent-crime-fugitive-arrests-lost-kidnapped-children" >news conference</a>, Boutros asserted judges would detain violent offenders at the first court appearance when the “numbers count" and then would release them at the second appearance. </p><p>Under the Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T Act, a judge can only detain offenders if the prosecutors file a petition. A hearing is held for the judge to consider the type of crime, the facts supporting the charge, the defendant's background and whether the defendant poses a threat to the community. A judge then decides if detention is warranted or the defendant should be subjected to electronic monitoring or home confinement.</p><p>Under the SAFE-T Act, the initial decision over detention is not a final determination. The SAFE-T Act allows prosecutors and defense the opportunity to file a motion challenging the judge’s decision.</p><p>Boutros, in his recent news conference, mentioned the judge who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/28/chicago-john-bartholomew-john-lyke-alphanso-talley-swedish-chicago-police-shooting" >released a man</a> on electronic monitoring before he allegedly went on to kill Chicago Police Officer John Bartholomew. Boutros also mentioned <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/11/19/terrorism-charges-filed-after-woman-lit-on-fire-on-blue-line-in-loop" >the man who allegedly set a young woman</a> on fire on the CTA's Blue Line. With these two tragic cases, a reasonable argument can be made that the judges exercised poor judgment in granting the release. But the reality is judges do not possess crystal balls to foresee the future.</p><p>Boutros needs to familiarize himself with Illinois Supreme Court Rules<a class="Link" href="https://ilcourtsaudio.blob.core.windows.net/antilles-resources/resources/f666b1cf-3509-4cf8-935e-ead5a1bb270d/RULE%203.8.pdf" target="_blank" > 3.8 (f) </a>and <a class="Link" href="https://ilcourtsaudio.blob.core.windows.net/antilles-resources/resources/a191b291-6103-48a8-b7f0-e7e7d0984080/RULE%203.6.pdf" target="_blank" >3.6 (a). </a></p><p>Rule 3.8 (f) provides, in part:</p><p>“The duty of a public prosecutor is to seek justice, not merely to convict. The prosecutor in a criminal case shall:</p><p> ...refrain from making extrajudicial comments that pose a serious and imminent threat of heightening public condemnation of the accused....”</p><p>Rule 3.6 (a) provides:</p><p>"A lawyer who is participating or has participated in the investigation or litigation of a matter shall not make an extrajudicial statement that the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated by means of public communication and would pose a serious and imminent threat to the fairness of an adjudicative proceeding in the matter.”</p><p>It is not a surprise Boutros would ignore such rules. Look at the improper prosecutorial actions committed under his watch related to the indictment in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >“Broadview Six”</a> case. One of his prosecutors had improperly vouched for the strength of the evidence before a grand jury and dismissed several members of the panel who were skeptical of the case. Boutros was forced to dismiss the case as a result.</p><p>Ironically, the prosecutorial misconduct was revealed only after his office tried trickery to hide it. His office initially tendered a grand jury redacted transcript to the judge for inspection — covering up the improper actions of the prosecutors.</p><p>When a prosecutor — the official sworn to uphold the constitutional safeguards of the criminal justice system — turns their ire upon the bench, they do not just breach professional responsibility duties; they fracture the bedrock of our justice system. Criticism is valid when it involves a failure to uphold the rule of law. However, personal attacks on members of the judiciary serve no useful purpose; they are tactical smokescreens designed to detract from the facts and inflame the public’s passions. </p><p>Lawyers and judges alike must remember that they are not gladiators in a theater of personal grievance but custodians of a delicate, sacred institution. Above all else, they must answer to the rule of law.</p><p><i>Daniel M. Locallo, retired Circuit Court of Cook County judge and former Cook County assistant state's attorney</i></p><h3>AI may not kill us, but it kills creativity </h3><p>I enjoy reading Neil Steinberg’s thoughtful columns even when I disagree. Case in point is his writing about the fear we have about new technology (<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/07/12/ai-artificial-intelligence-radio-technology-new-steinberg" >“Is AI going to kill us all? Radio, when new, also seemed a menace”</a>). I get his point. We often fear new technologies; albeit radio didn’t kill Lester Wolf — the careless use of electricity did.</p><p>The same danger faces us with artificial intelligence — its misuse, not the technology itself. What AI strips us of, when we allow it to do our thinking, is the process of self-discovery. </p><p>For example, when we allow AI to do our writing. The writing process is inextricably connected to thinking — thinking that is reflective of higher-order reasoning and self-knowledge. Good writing (and thinking) is at times contradictory, ambiguous, full of human emotion and nuanced. AI can’t deliver on that front.</p><p>What will “kill us” is allowing a technology tool to do our thinking for us. This is no illusionary risk. </p><p><i>Joe Burke, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Don’t be down on Deep Tunnel </h3><p>The negative tone of news coverage regarding Chicago's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/11/chicago-deep-tunnel-thornton-reservoir-flooding-calumet-south-suburbs-smell-mwrd-tarp-climate-change" >Deep Tunnel</a> following massive early July rains is baffling given its benefits, impact and history.</p><p>The Deep Tunnel is being ripped because the Thornton reservoir, when full, is smelly, the system’s rate of drainage is slow, and the capacity to handle runoff isn’t sufficient.</p><p>These attacks are overstated, and coverage of the Deep Tunnel lacks balance. In the 1970s and 1980s, coverage focused on flooded basements following heavy rains was frequent and cliché. Though basements still occasionally flood, they are minimal, thanks in part to the Deep Tunnel and the three reservoirs it feeds ahead of treatment.</p><p>Also, the Deep Tunnel was an inspiration for Milwaukee’s tunnel system and Indianapolis’ DigIndy project. Combined, these efforts have provided substantial environmental and health benefits to the urban Midwest.</p><p>More broadly, the 109-mile-long Deep Tunnel is an engineering marvel. </p><p>The reversal of the Chicago River and development of the skyscraper have been called engineering marvels of Chicago. The Deep Tunnel is also a wonder of modern engineering and deserves more appreciation.</p><p><i>Craig Barner, Lincoln Square</i></p><h3>Team owners care more about income streams</h3><p>I love how billionaire sports team owners say "we care about our fans," but put games on streaming services that a lot of fans don’t have. The only fans owners care about are Benjamin Franklins. No one can say that their viewership is higher compared to regular TV. How come a game can’t be on TV and streaming at the same time? This is exactly why a salary cap will only make owners richer while the majority of people can’t go to games. </p><p><i>Richard Orrico, Melrose Park</i></p><h3>Campaigns, casino cash shouldn’t mix</h3><p>Every American politician should be banned from taking campaign contributions from any casino group, owner or anyone with stock or financial interest in any casino or its entities. The reason is obvious, but we all know some politicians will continue to take contributions from casinos and give it to charity when the casino is investigated.</p><p><i>Richard Barber, Mount Greenwood</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Bride-to-be has given mixed signals to her inner circle
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have two best friends going back to third grade (we're in our 30s now) and one older sister. I'm the last in my friend group to get married. My fiancee and I are eloping this summer. We already own a house and need nothing, so I told my mother and sister that a bridal shower is unnecessary. Plus, since we are eloping, I felt it rude to invite people to a shower when no one would be invited to the elopement.</p><p>However, nobody has planned anything else for me. I understand people are busy with their own lives, but I always made time for them, and it makes me feel like I'm not important to them. It's becoming increasingly difficult not to feel slighted and forgotten.</p><p>I would have loved at least a fun girls' night at our favorite restaurant or even a quiet one watching chick flicks, wearing face masks and painting our toenails — a day where they said, "We thought about you." I worry that if I reach out to any of them about it, I'll sound like a spoiled brat. How can I manage these feelings? — <i>BRIDE, NOT BRAT</i></p><p><b>DEAR BRIDE:</b> Your friends and family are only doing exactly what you asked for. By eloping and refusing a bridal shower, you've signaled that you want this event to pass uncelebrated by the people closest to you. If that's not really what you want, speak up now.</p><p>I'm sure your friends and sister would love to show you how happy they are for you and shower you with well wishes. Approach one of your friends, apologize for the misunderstanding and give your permission for her to plan the girls' night you were hoping for (or plan it with her).</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I lent my friend an outfit and cardigan to wear to a wedding. Despite not wearing the cardigan, she washed it before returning it and ruined it. I didn't ask her not to wash it, and she didn't ask me if and how to wash it.</p><p>She has offered to pay for the cardigan, but it cost a lot more than she's used to paying for her clothes, so I feel bad that she's stuck paying for something she had no idea was expensive. What is the laundry etiquette in cases like this? Should I have told her to return it unwashed? Should she have asked how I would like it returned?</p><p>Should I ask her to reimburse me for it or is it just water under the bridge? She's a good friend, and I don't want to lose her over this, but I admit I am feeling resentful. — <i>DIRTY LAUNDRY IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DIRTY LAUNDRY:</b> Both of you are to blame for this: you for not specifying how you wanted your sweater returned, and her for not asking the question. Is the value of that sweater worth more than the friendship you have with this person? Because you know reimbursing you would be a stretch for her, why not chalk this up to an expensive lesson you learned?</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For everything you need to know about wedding planning, order "How to Have a Lovely Wedding." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Wedding Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Fillmore Linen Service brings jobs and opportunity to North Lawndale
entries.summary: <p>Ron Vann has spent nearly a third of his life behind bars.</p><p>The 58-year-old’s lengthy record of drug trafficking offenses have been a red flag for prospective employers his entire adult life.</p><p>Two years ago, he applied for a job at Fillmore Linen Service, a commercial laundry in North Lawndale serving the healthcare industry. The facility at 4100 W. Fillmore St. makes up a portion of the 168,000-square-foot Fillmore Center. </p><p>The center, along with Fillmore Linen, is funded by the Steans Family Foundation to create more opportunities in North Lawndale, where upward mobility has been stifled for generations by disinvestment, high unemployment and poverty rates and violent crime.</p><p>Vann was among the first workers hired at the company, which prioritizes employing formerly incarcerated job-seekers, recovering addicts and others largely overlooked by local employers because of prior transgressions.</p><p>He was promoted a few months ago to supervisor, overseeing more than 100 workers and being able to hire some staffers.</p><p>“This is truly one of the best things that ever happened to me,” the longtime North Lawndale resident said. “I could have been in jail for life. I could have been killed.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b60000" name="image-b60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f54f374/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eb49c4a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c7233f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of Fillmore Linen Serviceat 4100 W. Fillmore St." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c7233f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f399ed1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c7233f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7976x4476+0+102/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2Fc4%2F1a0b1263466b979b520955e3a2cf%2Ffillmore-260719-030.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Fillmore Linen Serviceat 4100 W. Fillmore St.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Vann’s eight gunshot wounds, one resulting in a lost kidney, attests to the latter. But his story of survival and redemption is similar to many of his coworkers.</p><p>“I have multiple employees that have been shot,” Fillmore Linen general manager Wendy McFall said. “This is normal for them. They live in an area where circumstances aren’t as favorable.”</p><p>Health, social and economic factors have exacerbated barriers for upward mobility in North Lawndale for decades, according to data from Opportunity Insights, a Harvard University research center that maps upward mobility metrics from childhood to middle age by neighborhood tracts.</p><p>Several areas within North Lawndale show more than half of those born in 1990 had incomes below the poverty line in 2015, at the time $11,770 for an individual and $24,250 for a family of four. In 2026, it's just under $16,000 for an individual and $33,000 for a family of four. The data also shows those who grew up in the West Side neighborhood are among the likeliest population in the city to go to jail or prison.</p><p>The life expectancy in the neighborhood is 70.7 years, the third lowest rate among Chicago’s 77 neighborhoods, according to statistics compiled from 2010-2024 by Chicago Health Atlas.</p><p>By comparison, three miles north, in Humboldt Park, life expectancy is 77.1 years, while Lake View has one of the city’s highest <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/11/20/death-gap-racial-life-expectancy-gap-west-garfield-park-heart-disease-cancer-homicide-opioid-overdose-chicago-west-side-loop" target="_blank" >life expectancy</a> rates, at 84.5 years, five years longer than Chicago's average.</p><p>North Lawndale also has some of the highest homicide, alcohol and drug-induced mortality rates in the city, Chicago Health Atlas data shows.</p><h3>Creating jobs</h3><p>North Lawndale was once a manufacturing hub for some of the city’s largest companies, including Western Electric, International Harvester and Sears Roebuck and Co., which established headquarters there in 1904. At its peak, the three companies employed more than 67,000 workers, occupying millions of square feet for production, packaging and distribution. </p><p>The neighborhood's population, fueled by the Great Migration of Black migrants, swelled to 125,000 by 1960. But the following decades were largely marked by plant closings and corporate relocations, resulting in massive job losses, growing poverty and blight. In 1966, the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. established his Chicago headquarters at a North Lawndale apartment to draw attention to degraded living conditions in America’s inner cities.</p><p>North Lawndale’s population today is about 34,000.</p><p>Fillmore Center, an economic hub that underwent a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/06/26/fillmore-linen-service-north-lawndale-project-jobs-steans-family-foundation" >three-year, $15 million renovation</a> by the Steans Family Foundation, was revived to reverse longtime trends in the area. The former home of Calumet Baking Powder Co. opened in 2024, with Fillmore Linen as its anchor tenant.</p><p>The laundry service has grown from a few dozen employees to more than 160. Its clients include Rush University System for Health, Lurie Children’s Hospital, St. Anthony Hospital and Shriners Children’s Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: What exactly would Trump's Triumphal Arch commemorate?
entries.summary: <p>If completed as planned, Donald Trump's triumphal arch outside Arlington National Cemetery will tower over the graceful Memorial Bridge, obstruct the view of the Lincoln Memorial from the cemetery (and vice versa), and offend anyone whose taste is north of Liberace.</p><p>But there's another aspect of this grotesquerie that deserves some attention: Namely, what is the triumph Trump is celebrating?</p><p>The Arch of Titus in Rome celebrates the Roman victory over the Jews and the sacking of Jerusalem in A.D. 70. </p><p>The Arch of Constantine honors Emperor Constantine's A.D. 315 victory in the Battle at the Milvian Bridge (before which Constantine supposedly saw a cross in the sky and therefore converted to Christianity). </p><p>The Arc de Triomphe in Paris was commissioned by Napoleon to commemorate his victory over the combined armies of Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in 1805. Whatever your view of imperial campaigns, military historians regard Napoleon's victory there as one of history's greatest. </p><p>Nelson's Column in London honors Horatio Nelson's defeat of the French and Spanish fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar. Nelson was mortally wounded, but his statue towers above the city he saved.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ef0000" name="module-ef0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>The U.S. has not traditionally gone in for victory monuments. We have a Washington Monument, but that's for the whole man, not the military victory. Same with the Lincoln Memorial, which stresses the terrible sacrifices the Civil War demanded. </p><p>There is a moving memorial at Pearl Harbor that remembers our dead and tells the story of our recovery. The tone is solemn. You can find a World War II memorial in Washington, but it's a tribute to the soldiers, sailors, airmen and others who fought the war, not a gloating expression of chauvinism.</p><p>The Dewey Monument in San Francisco honors the commodore who defeated the Spanish in Manila Bay, but it's the exception that proves the rule. </p><p>There is no victory arch for the Mexican-American War — though it was a crushing victory that doubled our territory. Americans felt queasy about celebrating it even in the 19th century. Ulysses Grant, who served in that war, recalled in his memoir: "I do not think there was ever a more wicked war than that waged by the United States on Mexico. I thought so at the time, when I was a youngster, only I had not moral courage enough to resign."</p><p>And the Vietnam Memorial is a mournful thing. A black granite trove of carved names, it memorializes the thousands of 15- to 62-year-olds who gave the last full measure of devotion to a nation that should never have gotten involved in that war with ground troops.</p><p>What victory is Trump memorializing? The great battle of Caracas that extracted a single man from his palace and left a repressive regime in place? Or is it the Iran War, clocking in at $132 billion so far, draining our munitions (that could have helped Ukraine) and leaving the regime in the hands of even more radical forces than before, a regime that now knows it has little to fear from the U.S. and has a powerful weapon in the Strait of Hormuz? A regime before which the Trump administration is dangling $300 billion of carrots for peace? When one side is offering reparations, who won?</p><p>The proposed Arc de Trump would dwarf the Arc de Triomphe in scale and destroy the geometry of the capital. The Memorial Bridge connects Arlington Cemetery and Robert E. Lee's former homestead to the Lincoln Memorial. It knits the former enemies back into one nation, but emphasizes that this is Lincoln's country now. His temple catches the sunlight.</p><p>After World War I, New York constructed a temporary Victory Arch of wood and plaster to welcome home the troops. There were plans to finish it in stone, but the funds never materialized, and it was allowed to crumble. That would be a just fate for Trump's monstrosity — but then again, wrecking cranes would be more efficient.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the "Beg to Differ" podcast. Her book, "Hard Right: The GOP's Drift Toward Extremism," is available now.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b00000" name="module-b00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago Public Schools coping with a staggering rise in special ed needs, costs
entries.summary: <p>Tiffany’s only baby was turning 2 when she decided that she couldn’t ignore a giant red flag: Her son had yet to utter a word, while other toddlers were putting together short sentences.</p><p>At her pediatrician’s urging, she was ready to have him evaluated to figure out what was going on.</p><p>What happened next gave her an early indication of what she would be up against as she tried to get her son support. Every clinic she called in the city had a long waiting list. It took a month to get an appointment and it was in northwest suburban Rolling Meadows, a nearly 40-mile drive from her South Side home.</p><p>When she finally got to meet with the psychiatrist on a video call a week later, she learned her son has autism.</p><p>“I didn’t really know what it meant at all and then there was a lot of sadness and grief,” Tiffany says now. She asked that her last name not be used to protect her son’s privacy.</p><p>But she told herself: “OK, we have to continue on, we have to figure this out and try to get him at his highest capacity, however that may look.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c50000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>When her son had reached his second birthday without uttering a single word, Tiffany decided to have him evaluated by a psychiatrist. He was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Tiffany’s little boy is now 6. And he is part of a growing group of students in Chicago Public Schools who have autism and need special education — a new reality for the school district that has major academic and financial implications.</p><p>As of this spring, almost 83,000 students qualified for either an individualized education program, known as an IEP, or a 504 plan, which legally require school districts to provide students with specialized education services or to remove barriers to their learning.</p><p>That’s 26% of CPS students, up from 20% in 2019. It’s a national trend that’s more pronounced in Chicago.</p><p>The number of students with autism has doubled since 2019, according to CPS data obtained through an open records request. Many of these students require intensive classroom support and therapy and a growing number spend the majority of their day in separate classes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-650000" name="html-embed-module-650000"></a><div style="min-height:495px" id="datawrapper-vis-RrYwS"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/RrYwS/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-RrYwS"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/RrYwS/full.png" alt="Surge in CPS students with autism and developmental delays (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Chicago is not alone. More children across the country are being diagnosed with autism, a fact that experts attribute to a variety of reasons, including that pediatricians and parents are more aware of the early signs.</p><p>Children with disabilities need these services to reach their full potential and are legally entitled to them. More than 50 years ago, a landmark federal law promised that students with disabilities would get a “free and appropriate education” and would no longer be left to languish in separate settings where they were scarcely educated.</p><p>But, as the cost of providing special education rises, federal and state funding is not keeping up. And that’s putting a tremendous strain on CPS’ and other districts’ budgets.</p><p>CPS spent $1.8 billion on special education in 2026, almost twice what it did in 2019. At the same time, the gap between what state and federal funding covers and what CPS must pay has grown by an astronomical amount. CPS’ total budget is roughly $10 billion.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-aa0000" name="html-embed-module-aa0000"></a><div style="min-height:439px" id="datawrapper-vis-Pbs7J"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Pbs7J/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Pbs7J"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Pbs7J/full.png" alt="Special education costs skyrocket, CPS burden rises (Stacked Bars)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Most of that money pays for teachers, aides, social workers, psychologists and therapists. It’s the primary reason why CPS added 9,000 staffers over the past seven years, even as its enrollment dropped by 45,000 students.</p><p>When CPS officials announced <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/15/cps-will-cut-teachers-and-five-student-non-attendance-days-as-district-looks-to-close-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>1,500 staff layoffs and other drastic measures</u></a> to close the district’s $732 million deficit earlier this week, they stressed that they were actually adding more special education staff.</p><p>Joshua Long, chief of CPS’ office for students with disabilities, said CPS is in a difficult position.</p><p>“We all know that meeting our legal obligations is not optional, and so as student needs evolve, our staffing resources must evolve with them,” he said.</p><p>School-level teams are charged with writing a legally binding plan that outlines what individual students need to learn and administrators must provide those resources. Efforts in the past to give students less than what school teams called for resulted in parent complaints, lawsuits and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2018/05/16/state-strips-cps-of-control-of-special-education" target="_blank" ><u>state monitoring of CPS’ special education program</u></a>.</p><p>“I don't really spend any time thinking about how we can cut staff to students with disabilities in schools,” Long says. “What I really spend time thinking about is, ‘are we doing the right thing?’”</p><h3>Special education trends converge at West Side elementary</h3><p>Over the last eight years, Nash Elementary in Austin has seen an eye-popping increase in students with disabilities and staff to support them. It’s not that unusual.</p><p>When Marcie Byrd became principal in 2018, Nash was like most other small neighborhood schools on Chicago’s West Side. The school had been losing students for two decades, almost all of its students were Black and it had no bilingual program. Byrd says she needs every member of her special education team.</p><p>“I might be a little pushy because they can’t really advocate for themselves,” she says of her students, “so we have to advocate for them.”</p><h3>State and federal funding for special education falls short</h3><p>In Illinois, schools get money for special education through the state’s overall funding formula for districts, with some additional funding for transportation and students who need services beyond what their public school can provide.</p><p>CPS says state special education funding is falling woefully short. And district leaders, school board members and unions are urgently calling on the state to increase funding. They want Gov. JB Pritzker or Democratic leaders to bring lawmakers in for a special session, but so far they have refused.</p><p>Pritzker’s office and state education officials say the state has stepped up its contributions to schools, primarily by putting $2.5 billion more into the education funding formula since Pritzker took office in 2019.</p><p>Still, two-thirds of school districts are well below the adequate funding level that the state promised to reach by next year. John Fetterman, who backed a bill last year to increase funding.</p><p>As a result, CPS relies on money from local taxpayers to ensure the district meets its legal obligations and students are properly served. It’s a necessity, but that limits what the district can spend on other aspects of education.</p><h3>As needs grow, more CPS students educated in separate classrooms</h3><p>Rush Medical Center on the Near West Side is inundated with calls from parents worried about their child’s development. Families usually have to wait months to get their child evaluated, says Cynthia Pierre, a clinical psychologist at Rush’s Autism Assessment, Research, Treatment & Services Center.</p><p>She knows parents, pediatricians and others “are really hungry to understand” why there are more autism diagnoses.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-real-reason-autism-rates-are-rising/" target="_blank" ><u>There’s not a simple answer</u></a>. Research has shown that autism is often heritable and that genetic variations and mutations play a role. But children are also at higher risk if their parents are older, their mom has poor mental health during pregnancy or they are born prematurely, Pierre says.</p><p>Likely the biggest change, though, is that pediatricians and parents are more aware of autism and are keyed in when children fail to hit developmental milestones, she says.</p><p>“We’re getting better at diagnosing subtle presentations of autism younger, especially with girls who tend to be overlooked,” Pierre says. “That can maybe explain, to some degree, why we're seeing kids come into the Chicago Public Schools with a diagnosis, as opposed to getting diagnosed later.”</p><p>CPS data bears this out: The rise in students in special education is most pronounced in preschool, kindergarten and first and second grades.</p><p>Jaunelle Pratt-Williams, a research scientist at NORC at the University of Chicago, a nonpartisan research organization, stresses that in the past, some disabilities were identified later, or not at all. So students remained in typical classrooms and did not receive the support they needed, often because their teachers lacked proper training and resources. When children get the right support earlier, it’s helpful for all students, she says.</p><p>“There’s a lot of research to support that strategic hiring of highly qualified educators makes a difference for students, and so, while it is expensive, there likely will be a positive outcome for students,” she says.</p><p>But as needs rise at certain grade levels, one CPS response is worrying advocates. CPS has opened many additional self-contained classrooms, which can provide students with added support, but are also more restrictive.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-290000" name="html-embed-module-290000"></a><div style="min-height:486px" id="datawrapper-vis-bTP3v"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/bTP3v/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-bTP3v"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/bTP3v/full.png" alt="More disabled students in separate classes (Stacked column chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>CPS added 60 last school year and is adding 60 more in the 2026-27 school year.</p><p>Barb Cohen, a legal advocate at Legal Council for Health Justice, which helps families access special education, says self-contained classes should mostly be for students with cognitive disabilities.</p><p>She worries some students with autism who don’t have a cognitive delay are being placed in separate classes because teachers and aides don’t know how to handle certain behaviors, such as meltdowns or communication issues. Self-contained classrooms typically span multiple grade levels, which can make it harder to hold students to the standards of their specific grade.</p><p>“It may not be what the kid needs. It may be what the teacher needs,” Cohen says. Especially “if the teacher doesn't feel like they're getting what they need to support this child” in a traditional setting.</p><p>Under federal law, students with disabilities are supposed to be placed in the least restrictive academic setting. Cohen says she’d like to see CPS provide specific training on how to work with children who are autistic, which could lessen placements in separate classes.</p><p>Overall, students with disabilities in CPS perform far worse than other students.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-160000" name="html-embed-module-160000"></a><div style="min-height:570px" id="datawrapper-vis-zu4Q3"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/zu4Q3/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-zu4Q3"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/zu4Q3/full.png" alt="Disabled students see academic gains but few meet state standard (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>That’s true at Nash Elementary. But Principal Byrd is proud of what she is able to offer her students. Last school year, two students who were in self-contained classes started spending the majority of their school day in classrooms with non-disabled peers.</p><p>“For other students, that may not be possible,” Byrd says. “I want to see growth for all of the kids, whatever that growth looks like for each individual child. They may be fifth grade, but they may not be able to talk, so the goal is maybe we teach them how to talk. That is a big deal for them.”</p><h3>CPS adds staff but many parents still see gaps in support</h3><p>Despite the increase in special education staff, many CPS parents, teachers and advocates say it’s still too difficult to get students all the help they need. entries.title: Man killed in Fuller Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was killed in a shooting early Saturday in Fuller Park on the South Side. </p><p>The man, 25, was standing outside in the 4800 block of South Princeton Avenue when someone opened fire around 2:55 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>The man was shot in the head and was taken to Provident Hospital of Cook County, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His name hasn't been released. </p><p>No arrests have been made. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Person injured during struggle with cops at large gathering in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>A person was injured during a struggle over a gun with Chicago police officers early Saturday in Fuller Park on the South Side. </p><p>Officers assigned to the 9th District Tactical Team responded to a call of a large gathering in the 5300 block of South Princeton Avenue around 12:30 a.m. and attempted to disperse a crowd, Chicago police said. </p><p>While attempting to break up the crowd, officers stopped a person for possible possession of a gun, police said. During a brief physical struggle, the person's gun discharged and they were shot in the thigh. </p><p>Officers called for an ambulance and the person was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in good condition, police said. </p><p>The officers did not fire their weapons and no other injuries were reported, police said. </p><p>The Investigative Response Team is working the case.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Person arrested for fatally shooting man who stabbed woman in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A person was arrested after fatally shooting a man who allegedly stabbed another woman Friday night in Englewood on the South Side. </p><p>A 22-year-old woman and a man were arguing inside a home in the 400 block of West Marquette Road around 10:55 p.m. when the man pulled out a sharp object and stabbed the woman in the abdomen, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man, 36, then pulled the 22-year-old outside of the home, according to police.</p><p>Police said a female inside the home, whose age wasn't known, witnessed the altercation and shot the man in the chest. He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. His name hasn't been released. </p><p>The 22-year-old was taken to the same hospital in good condition, police said. </p><p>Officers arrested the female and recovered the gun, police said. Charges were pending. </p>

On the ground, you can sense the smoke and maybe see hints of it in the distance, but you don't grasp its full density until you take a step back and see it from afar. I chose that vantage point specifically to frame the Ferris wheel in the foreground, using it as a point of reference aiming back toward the city skyline. entries.title: Runners turn out for Chinatown 5K after days of poor air quality
entries.summary: <p>More than 850 runners</p><p> joined the 20th anniversary of the Chinatown 5K on Saturday, undeterred by days of hazardous air quality that caused <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/16/air-quality-outdoor-events-canceled-list-concerts-beaches" target="_blank" ><u>cancellations</u></a> of many outdoor events in Chicago.</p><p>On Thursday, smoke from Canadian wildfires cloaked the Chicago area in a thick, uncanny haze. Government agencies issued <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" target="_blank" ><u>health warnings</u></a> and urged people to stay indoors. Although conditions improved by Friday afternoon, some parks and venues <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/17/air-quality-alert-extends-into-day-two-as-wildfire-smoke-from-canada-shuts-down-beaches-venues-citywide" target="_blank" ><u>remained closed</u></a>.</p><p>Race organizers with the Chinatown nonprofit Project: Vision monitored the air quality and weather until early Saturday morning ahead of the 5K’s 8 a.m. start time, followed by a 9 a.m. youth run.</p><p>Karen Chiu, founder and executive director for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/07/16/chinatown-5k-race-800-runners-historic-neighborhood" target="_blank" ><u>Project: Vision</u></a>, said organizers “were juggling excitement with close monitoring. The team worked to weigh the risks and benefits of keeping it going versus canceling.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Connor Bedard signs new five-year contract with Blackhawks
entries.summary: <p>Connor Bedard has set himself up for a possibly gargantuan payday in 2031 after signing a new five-year contract with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>.</p><p>The Hawks presumably pushed for an eight-year maximum-length contract in negotiations, but they ultimately agreed Saturday to a bridge deal with a $15 million salary-cap hit.</p><p>The shorter term helps keep the cap hit semi-reasonable compared to Ducks star Leo Carlsson's new $18 million cap hit. However, Bedard, who just turned 21 on Friday, is now slated to become an unrestricted free agent at the end of the contract.</p><p>"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and [he] has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement.</p><p>"He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat but [also] to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."</p><p>The Hawks will have to figure out a way to re-sign Bedard again down the road — and it might be even more difficult then — but that's a problem for another day. They'll also have to build a team around his huge cap hit, but that also isn't an imminent issue — and might never become a major issue given how quickly the NHL salary cap is rising.</p><p>The most important thing was locking up the centerpiece of their new generation without a holdout — or the worst-case scenario of an offer sheet — and that crucial to-do item has now been checked off.</p><p>Bedard's first three Hawks seasons have been remarkably similar to Patrick Kane's first three seasons. Bedard has 203 points in his first 219 games; Kane also tallied 203 points in his first 219 games.</p><p>Now, Bedard has also followed in Kane's footsteps with the bridge-deal concept coming off his entry-level contract. Kane signed for five years at $6.3 million per year starting in 2010-11, then cashed in with an eight-year deal at $10.5 million per year starting in 2015-16.</p><p>Bedard's big step forward in 2025-26 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/30/blackhawks-connor-bedard-nhl-creating-space-nikita-kucherov-jeff-blashill" target="_blank" >squashed</a> any concerns about him not reaching his elite ceiling as he reached the 30-goal and 75-point marks in 69 games.</p><p>He tied for 20th in the NHL in points per game and likely would've ranked higher if not for an injury-hampered January. He also likely would've ranked higher if he had any sort of quality linemates, which he theoretically should gain during the course of this new contract.</p><p>Bedard won't be able to start this coming season on time, however, after undergoing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/08/blackhawks-connor-bedard-shoulder-surgery-injury-timeline" target="_blank" >left shoulder surgery</a> following an injury in practice earlier this month. He's slated to return in early to mid-November, missing the first 15-20 games of the season.</p><p>Kane, coincidentally, is back on the Hawks' radar now, with Chris Chelios telling 670 The Score last week that Kane told him he's currently deciding between contract offers from the Hawks and Sabres. That's one more notable piece of business for Davidson to figure out, as are contracts for still-restricted free agents Kevin Korchinski and Ethan Del Mastro.</p><p><i>This story will be updated.</i></p>

entries.title: Why Anthony Rizzo says 'it was never disappointing' Cubs didn't follow 2016 with more championships
entries.summary: <p>When the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> won the 2016 World Series, it looked like it could have been the start of a dynasty. Key players were young, there was money to spend and the group showed it could survive any challenge.</p><p>Instead, the Cubs are celebrating the 10th anniversary of the lone ring of that era. To some, that might be a disappointment, that the <b>Theo Epstein-</b>assembled core only made it back to the National League Championship Series in 2017 and was broken up in 2021.</p><p><b>Anthony Rizzo </b>doesn’t see it that way.</p><p>“It was never disappointing,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/06/25/chicago-cubs-anthony-rizzo-bob-costas-jason-benetti-bruce-cornblatt-roger-clemens-will-middlebrooks-david-ross-yankees-red-sox-nbc-sunday-night-baseball" >Rizzo</a> said Saturday at the dedication of Champions Gate. “It’s really hard to win in this game.”</p><p>In 2015 and 2016, the Cubs made it look easy. They won a combined 200 regular-season games and reached consecutive NLCS. Then things got harder, some players departed, others stagnated and the window shut.</p><p>“The teams are never the same,” Rizzo said. “We did have a good core and we did a lot of special things in that four, five, six-year run but winning in this game, winning every day, winning a ballgame on July 18 against the Minnesota Twins is not easy. You have to cherish every one of them.”</p><p>That’s one of the perspectives Epstein has picked up in the last decade.</p><p>“It’s one thing to assemble a bunch of talent, it’s another thing to have that group turn into a championship team that stands up in the face of adversity at the most important times,” Epstein said.</p><p>The 2016 group is not going down in history like the 1990s Bulls or even the 2010s Blackhawks. Like the 1985 Bears, they were one-and-done even though they looked like a team that could win multiple times.</p><p>That hasn’t diminished what they mean to Cubs fans.</p><p>“Whether it’s in Chicago, in Illinois, or nationwide or worldwide, we get told stories on a daily or weekly basis of what this meant to families and generations of families, and that’s special,” <b>Jake Arrieta</b> said. “This is something we were able to do and cement ourselves in Cubs history forever.”</p><h2>Russell attends</h2><p>One of the 2016 alumni in attendance was starting shortstop <b>Addison Russell</b>.</p><p>Between 2018 and 2019, Russell served a 40-game suspension for violating MLB’s domestic-abuse policy. In September 2018, MLB put Russell on administrative leave after an investigation into abuse allegations detailed by his ex-wife, <b>Melisa Reidy-Russell</b>.</p><p>“Today we celebrated the players who made significant contributions to the Cubs’ 2016 World Championship team. As the organization stated publicly in 2019, Addison took accountability for his actions, served his suspension, and completed an extensive rehabilitation process before returning to play for the Cubs later that season,” Cubs spokesperson <b>Jennifer Martinez-Roth </b>said in a statement to the Sun-Times.</p><p>Russell, who also attended the 2026 Cubs Convention, went through MLB-mandated treatment and voluntary counseling during his suspension. He was cheered when he was introduced at both the Champions Gate dedication and before the game inside Wrigley Field.</p><h2>Dansby in</h2><p>Shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson </b>started and hit eighth, a day after getting hit in the face by a deflected throw on an attempted double play.</p>

entries.title: Chicago sees slight air quality improvement, but smoky, hazy conditions persist
entries.summary: <p>After days of wildfire smoke blanketing the Chicago area, air quality improved Saturday, though it remained unclear when the lingering haze would fully clear.</p><p>Air quality reached the "moderate" category Saturday, but an air quality alert remained in effect through Saturday night, according to the National Weather Service. Forecasters warned that conditions could deteriorate again later in the day as smoke concentrations fluctuate.</p><p>“The general expectation is for a gradual deterioration in air quality through the night,” said Jake Petr, meteorologist at the weather service.</p><p>The smoky haze is expected to linger through the weekend and into Monday, Petr said. Beyond that, the forecast remains uncertain because wildfire smoke will continue drifting into the region as fires burn in Canada and Minnesota. As long as those fires remain active, smoky conditions could persist.</p><p>Chicago experienced its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-air-quality-kn95-mask-sales" target="_blank" ><u>worst air quality Thursday</u></a>, when wildfire smoke pushed the city into the ranks of the world's most polluted major cities. The weather conditions prompted city officials to close the beaches and several events throughout the area were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/16/air-quality-outdoor-events-canceled-list-concerts-beaches" target="_blank" >canceled</a>. </p><p>Beaches and city pools reopened Friday afternoon, though the Chicago Park District said programming would be moved indoors. The Garfield Park Conservatory, Lincoln Park Conservatory and the Morton Arboretum in suburban Lisle were also open Saturday. </p><p>Petr urged residents to check the air quality before going outside and to protect themselves by wearing masks. Those with breathing issues should remain indoors.</p><p>In addition to the smoke, thunderstorms with wind gusts of up to 60 mph were possible Saturday, which saw rain showers roll through the Chicago area in the morning and early afternoon. However, rain would do little to clear the smoky conditions, Petr said.</p><p>Sunny conditions were expected Sunday, but lingering smoke is likely to remain as temperatures dip into the low 80s.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" >‘Hazardous’ Canadian wildfire smoke prompts air quality warning for Chicago. Here’s what you should know.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Swiss Army Schweitz: Rookie reliever Tyler Schweitzer proving versatile for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>TORONTO — Rookie reliever Tyler Schweitzer was pleasantly surprised to look up at the scoreboard to see the official scorer had credited him with his first career win, after Schweitzer pitched three scoreless innings to close the Sox’ 12-4 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/17/white-sox-toronto-braden-montgomery-murakami-derby" target="_blank" ><u>blowout win</u></a> on Friday.</p><p>“I was thinking I was going to get the save,” a beaming Schweitzer said. It was left to the scorer’s discretion because starter Anthony Kay only went four innings. “I was like, ‘Oh, let’s go!’ First one.”</p><p>The Indianapolis native notched his first career save in unorthodox fashion last month with four impressive innings that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/30/white-sox-colson-montgomery-home-run-orioles" target="_blank" ><u>sealed a win in Baltimore</u></a>.</p><p>“Really impressive stuff,” manager Will Venable said. “To get the coverage is one thing, but to get the quality is another thing, and he puts those together. He's really valuable for us.”</p><p>What’s the next box Schweitzer (2.77 ERA in 13 innings) wants to check? “Honestly, just keep winning and hopefully pop some bottles.”</p><div class="Enhancement" I just keep working and making my adjustments,” he said.</p><h3><b>Gonzalez’s greener pastures</b></h3><p>Jacob Gonzalez was still helping the Sox a week after general manager Chris Getz <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/11/white-sox-use-pitching-defense-to-beat-athletics-1-0" target="_blank" ><u>dealt him</u></a> and reliever Brandon Eisert to Pittsburgh in exchange for Triple-A reliever and the draft pick the Sox used to take <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/12/chicago-white-sox-mlb-draft-landon-thome-jim-thome-roch-cholowsky-andrew-benintendi-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>Landon Thome</u></a>.</p><p>Gonzalez swatted a two-run homer on a 2-for-4 afternoon to power the Pirates past the Guardians 7-1 Saturday, keeping the Sox a half-game ahead in the American League Central. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jacob Gonzalez's first <a href="https://x.com/Pirates?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Pirates</a> homer is a 428-foot blast! <a href="https://t.co/ujg9RkCgMF">pic.twitter.com/ujg9RkCgMF</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2078533611909751182?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Tristan Peters returns to Canada as an All-Star in his breakout season for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>TORONTO — Tristan Peters checked another box off his list this weekend during a stunning breakout season for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>.</p><p>In a year of improbable firsts for the rookie anchoring center field, Peters returned to his native Canada this weekend as an All-Star playing his first big-league games north of the border.</p><p>The Sox’ series in Toronto isn’t exactly a homecoming for the 26-year-old, whose hometown of Winkler, Manitoba, is about 500 miles closer to Rate Field than it is to the Rogers Centre.</p><p>But it means a lot to the rangy, grinding outfielder who has vaulted himself from an offseason afterthought to a stalwart for the White Sox on both sides of the ball.</p><p>“This is obviously the country I was born in, and it has a special place in my heart,” said Peters, who played a youth tournament under the retractable roof in Toronto as a high schooler. “I've dreamed of playing in this stadium, too. It's one of my favorite ballparks.”</p><p>“It was a special team when I was growing up and I loved watching them,” Peters said, idolizing the likes of Jose Bautista and Kevin Pillar, whose high-flying defensive prowess helped model a Canadian youngster’s game. “I liked the way he played the outfield,” Peters said.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div> </div></div><p>Peters, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/11/white-sox-outfielder-tristan-peters-named-to-al-all-star-team" target="_blank" ><u>hit for the cycle</u></a> earlier this month, ranks among the top three qualified rookies in batting average (.297), doubles (20) and triples (3). He’s also tagged three homers while posting an .817 OPS that no one saw coming out of spring training.</p><p>Like most fans, manager Will Venable knew next to nothing about Peters before the Sox acquired him from Tampa Bay for a proverbial bucket of baseballs.</p><p>“Right away, there [were] objectively projections that really liked him against right-handed pitching,” Venable said. “We had high expectations for him, but certainly not this. He’s performing really well defensively, obviously at the plate as well. And he’s great in the clubhouse.”</p><p>More importantly, he’s kept up with big-league pitchers who are still trying to find weaknesses to exploit.</p><p>“He's really made adjustments at the plate with our hitting coaches and made adjustments defensively with his pre-pitch and some of the stuff he's trying to do out there,” Venable said. “He's obviously having a lot of success, but has made a lot of adjustments and worked really hard to get there.”</p><p>The only thing that might’ve seemed more far-fetched than Peters’ All-Star ascent in February might’ve been the idea that the Sox would be sitting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/16/chicago-white-sox-chris-getz-will-venable-mlb-trade-deadline-blue-jays" >in first place in late July</a>.
